deep.reconstruction:
Context: E598 sets out a general procedure for finding which residues mod 4n contain the prime divisors of p²±nq². Here Euler finishes the case n=30 and starts n=−30.

(1) End of Exemplum 10, divisors of F = pp+30qq (discriminant −120). On the previous page the reduction step (g = 0..3, fh = 30+g²) gave four kinds of divisor: D=F, 2D=F, 3D=F, 5D(=6D)=F. In modern terms these are the four reduced forms x²+30y², 2x²+15y², 3x²+10y², 5x²+6y². He adds a remark:
- 2D=F implies 15D=F, because 15(2x²+15y²) = (15y)²+30x².
- 3D=F implies 10D=F, and 5D=F implies 6D=F, in the same way.

(2) Corollary 2 (§34). Every divisor lies in a class 120i+a, but not every number 120i+a is a divisor. One must first remove numbers divisible by some prime of the excluded classes 120i+α. Euler then states as 'maxime probabile' that all remaining numbers, and in particular all primes ≡ a (mod 120), do divide some p²+30q². In modern terms: a prime p∤30 divides some x²+30y² with gcd(x,y)=1 exactly when (−30/p)=1. This follows from quadratic reciprocity (Legendre; Gauss 1801). He lists the entries 1, 11, …, 233 up to 240; apart from the unit 1 these are all prime.

(3) Corollary 3 (§35). The 16 admissible residues mod 120 are sorted by the form that represents them:
- class 1: 1, 31, 49, 79
- class 2: 17, 23, 47, 113
- class 3: 13, 37, 43, 67
- class 6: 11, 29, 59, 101
Euler notes that each class occurs exactly four times. In modern terms, the genus characters for discriminant −120 split the 16 residues into 4 genera of 4. Each genus contains exactly one class (h(−120)=4, class group (Z/2)²), so 30 is one of Euler's idoneal numbers.

(4) Exemplum 11 (§36): divisors of p²−30q² (equivalently 30p²−q²), discriminant +120.
- The bound √(30/5) < 3 is the Lagrange-type reduction bound for indefinite forms. If 2|B| ≤ |A|, |C| then B² ≤ n/5, so g = 0, 1, 2.
- g=0 gives r²−30s², 2r²−15s², 3r²−10s², 5r²−6s².
- g=1 gives (r+s)²−30s², the proposed form itself.
- g=2 gives (r+2s)²−30s² and 2r²+4rs−13s². The latter has double 2(2r²+4rs−13s²) = (2r+2s)²−30s².
- He concludes there are four kinds: D=F, 2D=F, 3D=F, 6D=F.
- He then begins listing the candidates a = p², p²/2, p²/3, p²/6 mod 120. This continues on the next page, where he finds that, once signs are allowed, the classes merge into two.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page. The residue table and its class labels check out (e.g. 11=5+6, 29=5+24, 59=5+54, 101=5+96; 43=3+40, 67=27+40; 23=8+15, 113=98+15).
The prime list up to 240 is complete and correct. 1 is included as the unit, as Euler habitually does.
Minor inconsistency of labelling: the fourth class is called '5D=F' in §33 but marked '6' in §35. Euler himself notes the two are equivalent.
The claim in §34 is stated only as 'maxime probabile' (unproved). It is true by quadratic reciprocity.

ideas.what: Classification of divisors of x²+30y² into four types D, 2D, 3D, 5D/6D represented by the form, i.e. the four reduced forms of discriminant −120
ideas.modern_name: reduced binary quadratic forms / class group of discriminant −120
ideas.where_published: Euler's divisor papers on pp+nqq (e.g. E164, E256) and the idoneal-number papers (E708, E725)

ideas.what: Each of the four classes accounts for exactly 4 of the 16 residues mod 120
ideas.modern_name: genus theory; one class per genus (30 idoneal)

ideas.what: Conjecture that every prime ≡ a (mod 120) divides some p²+30q²
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler conjecture; proofs by Legendre and Gauss

ideas.what: Bound g ≤ √(n/5) for reducing divisors of p²−nq²
ideas.modern_name: reduction of indefinite binary quadratic forms

deep.surprise_reason: This is a worked example of Euler's standard divisor/genus computation for n=30 (an idoneal number). Everything here is well known and subsumed by Lagrange–Gauss theory.
transcription_corrections: The radical in §36 is plausibly √(30/5) < 3, i.e. the bound for indefinite forms (√6 ≈ 2.45). This is consistent with g = 0, 1, 2.
